title: Hear, O Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4)
hook: the Shema is said with a hand over the eyes, attention on one thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tallit, and the four fringes gathered into one hand. Your line was gather the corners. Who did you bring a little closer? Today, holding those fringes, the Shema itself. Day five hundred sixty-six.

The Torah itself says when to say these words: when you lie down, and when you rise up. So they're said every morning and every night, and at bedtime too. The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva, dying, said them, and drew out the last word until his breath ran out. Six Hebrew words. And when the moment comes to say them in the service, something unusual happens. People don't look up. They don't look at the book. Many raise a hand and cover their eyes, and for a few seconds the world goes dark for them.
screen: `MORNING, NIGHT AND BEDTIME.` → `SIX HEBREW WORDS.` → `A HAND OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation, Deuteronomy six reads: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. The Hebrew has no word for is, so translators have put this verse into English in more than one way, but the heart of it is clear: one. Start with the first word. Shema means hear. But in Hebrew it stretches wider: to listen, to understand, to take to heart, even to obey. And notice who's being spoken to. It isn't addressed to God. It's addressed to Israel, to the people. A declaration, said to each other and to yourself. Now the hand. The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, says that Rabbi Judah the Prince, when he reached this verse, would pass his hand over his eyes. The custom of covering the eyes grows from that. Close off everything you can see, and attend to one thing. The same page of the Talmud praises those who draw out the last word, echad, one, long enough to mean it. And in a Torah scroll, two letters of this verse are written large: the last letter of shema, an ayin, and the last letter of echad, a dalet. Together they spell ed, witness. Commentators read that as a hint: whoever says this line stands as a witness. Hear, in this reading, means more than ears: the whole of the attention, gathered, like the four fringes in one hand.
screen: `SHEMA YISRAEL: HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `HEAR, LISTEN, TAKE TO HEART.` · `A HAND OVER THE EYES.` · `AYIN AND DALET: WITNESS.` · then, large: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: cover your eyes and say it. Settle, and breathe. Raise your right hand and rest it over your eyes. Let the dark settle. Notice whether everything seems quieter when you can't see it. If you're Jewish, or you'd like to, say the six words slowly: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. Draw out the last word. If not, simply listen in the dark. Count the sounds you hear, then let them go, until there's just your breath. One thing. The bell holds the time.
Hear. Shema: listen, understand, take to heart. The first word of Judaism's central declaration.
Your line: hear, o israel. Today, when someone speaks to you, put everything else down, and hear them with your whole attention. Day five hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Jews say the Shema in the morning and evening services and at bedtime; for the first verse, many cover their eyes with the right hand and draw out the word echad, and the line is traditionally said at the end of life.

options: cover their eyes with a hand.
fork.reveal: many cover their eyes, as Rabbi Judah the Prince did in the Talmud, to shut out everything else and attend to one thing.

original.note: Hebrew: hear, listen, understand. the first word of Deuteronomy 6:4.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer to God.
what it means: a declaration to the people, said with eyes covered, attention gathered on one.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 13b on covering the eyes and drawing out echad; the enlarged ayin and dalet of the Masoretic scribal tradition, read as ed, witness.

sources.quoted: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one.

notes: Deuteronomy 6:4 quoted from JPS 1917; verify punctuation.
Berakhot 13b: Rabbi (Judah the Prince) passing his hand over his face/eyes; prolonging echad (Symmachus); confirm.
Enlarged ayin and dalet in the Torah scroll, read as 'ed' (witness), e.g. Baal HaTurim; confirm attribution to 'commentators'.
'No word for is' and range of translations: neutral statement; confirm.
Practice invites saying the Hebrew 'if you're Jewish, or you'd like to'; confirm phrasing is welcoming and appropriate.

Editor review: hook's unsourced 'the first prayer many Jewish children learn' and 'what many Jews have tried to say as their last words' replaced with Deuteronomy 6:7 (paraphrased) and Berakhot 61b (Rabbi Akiva's death with echad); 'people have done it ever since' and the closing imperative to the listener softened. Keeper: confirm Berakhot 61b retelling.
